name: Nose strips for nose shape

card.summary: Silicone clips worn on the nose that are marketed to lift the tip and slim the bridge for a sharper-looking profile without surgery.
card.aka: Nose lifter, nose shaper clip, nose slimming clip
card.note: Continuous pressure can irritate skin; no study has tested effectiveness or safety.

quick.overview:
Nose shaper clips are small silicone or plastic clips or clamps that sit on the nose and apply gentle pressure. Sellers describe them as a non-surgical way to lift a drooping tip, narrow the nostrils or slim the bridge.

The appearance goal is a slimmer, more lifted nose. Manufacturers say 10 to 30 minutes a day brings change, while an explainer cited here says adult cartilage and bone are not reshaped by external pressure and that no scientific study supports effectiveness or safety.
quick.how: Users wear the clip for set periods each day, often while at home. Some pair it with makeup contouring; reviewers also mention use after rhinoplasty, which the explainer advises against.
quick.risks: Pressure may cause redness, irritation or, rarely, tissue damage. Internal models can cause mucosal infection and the explainer warns teenagers are at higher risk.

lead: Nose shaper clips are small devices of soft silicone or plastic, sometimes on a metal frame, that clamp the nose or sit inside the nostrils. They are sold as a way to slim the bridge, narrow nostrils or lift the tip [1].

Marketing says 10 to 30 minutes a day gradually reshapes cartilage, with some sellers promising results in two weeks [1]. The idea is an old one: Victorian London perfumer Alexander Ross sold a nose-shaping machine in 1871 and 1872 [2], and nonsurgical nasal augmentation has been documented in early 20th-century Korea [3].

chain: Clip applies steady pressure to bridge or tip
Slimmer or more lifted nose profile
angle.text: People wear the clip daily hoping for a narrower bridge or a lifted tip. Any change is claimed by sellers; the effect has not been tested in a published study.

infobox: Cosmetic gadget; no clinical validation found [1]

paras: Designs include external clamps, U-shaped clips for the bridge and intranasal splints. They are also sold as nose shrinkers, sharpeners or lifters [1].

Manufacturers say regular use narrows nostrils, reduces a slight bump and lifts a drooping tip. One medical explainer says adult bone and cartilage cannot be reshaped by external pressure, that cartilage tends to return to its form after removal, and that no scientific study validates these devices [1]. It lists makeup contouring, temporary hyaluronic acid fillers (about 12 to 18 months) and rhinoplasty as other routes to a changed profile [1].

The explainer lists restricted blood flow causing redness, irritation or rarely tissue necrosis, mucosal infection from intranasal models, possible cartilage weakening or asymmetry, and higher risk in teenagers. It says the clips do not treat a deviated septum and should not be used after rhinoplasty [1].

In 1871 to 1872 Alexander Ross advertised a nose machine to shape the nose when worn an hour a day, priced at 10s. 6d. [2]. A 2024 study examined nasal profile ideals and nonsurgical augmentation methods in Korea in 1910 to 1945 [3].

timeline.event: Alexander Ross introduces a nose-shaping machine in London [2].
Nonsurgical nasal augmentation and camouflage makeup discussed in Korean media [3].
